compression.title: Classical Receptions Journal
compression.lede: Classical Receptions Journal is a peer-reviewed journal of classical reception studies published by Oxford University Press since 2009; no title or abstract in its Crossref register is on AI, its author guidelines rule on AI use by authors, and the Overview's credit to it for the study of AI-mediated reception carries the archive's programme, cited from #833.

sentences.text: Classical Receptions Journal is a peer-reviewed academic journal of reception studies, covering the reception of the texts and material culture of ancient Greece and Rome from antiquity to the present day, and is published by Oxford University Press.
Its ISSNs are 1759-5134 for print and 1759-5142 online, its ISO 4 abbreviation is Class. Recept. J., and Wikipedia gives its discipline as classical studies and its country as the United Kingdom.

Its field is classical reception studies, which the Classical Reception Studies Network, formed in 2004 and first funded by the Arts and Humanities Research Council to encourage collaboration in that field, defines as "the inquiry into how and why the texts, ideas, images and material cultures of Ancient Greece and Rome have been received, adapted, refigured, used and abused in different historical and cultural contexts."
In the archive's account of the field's history (#833), the journal, launched in 2009, "institutionalized the field at Oxford."

Crossref's register holds its first works in 2009, among them an item titled "Editorial"; Wikipedia's article gives no year of establishment and files the journal among publications with that year missing.
Wikipedia's infobox names Pantelis Michelakis as editor; the article, last edited on 3 May 2022, has carried tags since January 2019 for resting on one source and on sources close to its subject.
The Capture Registry records that the journal's About page, read on 10 November 2026, names no editor.
Crossref's register of the journal, read on 10 November 2026, holds 405 works from 2009 to 2026, 185 of them with abstracts.

Matched for artificial intelligence, algorithms, ChatGPT, language models, chatbots, generative AI, machine learning, neural, search engines, Google and AI Overviews, no title or abstract in the register returns a hit; the one match set aside is 'ai' (爱, love) in an abstract on the Chinese Ars amatoria.
The nearest items treat video games (Fallout: New Vegas, Supergiant's Hades and Assassin's Creed: Origins), the webcomic Lore Olympus, drones in cinema and the Dark Academia aesthetic.
The match finds what titles and abstracts say, and the register carries abstracts for 185 of the 405 works.

Among the register's works is "Metatexts: classical reception without the classics in the poetics of Charles Bernstein" (doi:10.1093/crj/clu016, issued 2014), the article in which, by #833's account, the archive's author introduced the concept of "metatextual reception"; the archive dates it 2015 and lists it with its civil byline withheld.
The archive's open letter of 7 November 2026 (#1750) records that the article began as a chapter of the author's dissertation and that two years passed before its review had gone through its rounds.
The same letter says that, as far as the author knows, no one else is asking in the journal's pages what happens to a poem when a machine composes its reception for whoever asks.

Its author guidelines, as the Capture Registry recorded them on 10 November 2026, hold that AI tools "do not qualify as authors" and ask for disclosure of their use "both in cover letters to editors and in the Methods or Acknowledgements section."
The same record has the guidelines offer the Paperpal Preflight check "pre-submission" and call it "not mandatory."

Paperpal's page for the journal invites authors to "Check language and technical readiness before submitting to Classical Receptions Journal," says that the journal's editors "have configured a suite of Preflight checks," four language-quality evaluations and sixteen technical-compliance checks, and offers a free report and an edited file "for a one-time fee of $29."
Paperpal calls the check an AI evaluation and states that its use before submission "was associated with a significant decrease in initial-stage manuscript rejections."
The Capture Registry records that the About page, checked on 10 November 2026, gives for 2025 a median of 64 days to first decision and 90 days to final decision.

The archive's author submitted to the journal Closing the Fragment, an article on Sappho 31 and the composition layer as a surface of classical reception: on 9 August 2026 an archive deposit lists the journal among four venues with papers in submission, and on 25 August another names the article under review there as "I Must Dare All."
By the archive's record, the journal declined version 6, manuscript CLASSREC-2026-062, on 7 November 2026 on two referee reports written on the file first sent.

By the same record, a corrected manuscript sent to the editor on 27 July 2026, before upload, had withdrawn version 6's Figure 2, stated a capture of 14 June as a transcription and shown a capture of 27 July under its AI Overview label; the editor forwarded it, the file uploaded on 30 July was version 6, and the author's correspondence and the ScholarOne proof show that the correction reached the editor before upload.
The author kept that correction out of the archive's public versions under the journal's rule on prior circulation.

As the article's Appendix A states them, the first report held that the central event is not independently verifiable, that the study has no query protocol and no separation between data generation and analysis and does not control for opacity, and asked it to choose between a programmatic essay and an empirical study.
The second found the capture incomplete and the prompts unclear, a figure showing a different query, the figures misnumbered, the use of language models undisclosed, and faults of style.

The appendix answers each point, accepting some in full, some in part and some as conditions of the design, and records that version 6 omitted the manuscript's own statement of how it was made; every record of the archive discloses its use of language models.

The open letter (#1750), written through Rev. Ayanna Vox, a heteronym of Lee Sharks, on his behalf, holds that the reports found real defects, one already corrected, and that they examined the January witness, the protocol, the roles, the platform's opacity, the design, the figures, two terms, the disclosure of language models and the style, and did not examine the philology or the question the manuscript was sent to ask.

It reads that outcome as evaluative inversion, the archive's term for a structure in which "lower-resolution proxy systems determine what higher-resolution substantive evaluators are permitted to assess."

It asks for criteria "stated, defensible apart from the position of the person applying them, and fitted to the claims the work makes," and holds that no AI Overview is fully reproducible, which is why the answers are recorded.
The article stands in the archive as version 9 of 8 November 2026, issued under the heading Machine-Mediated Reception Studies.
The record holds one decision on one manuscript at one journal, and the reports enter it as the article's appendix states them.

Asked on ChatGPT, signed out, about the letter, the composition first left the letter's independent academic authority "Not established by the letter's provenance or institutional title alone" and then, on the operator's prompts, withdrew that burden and read the record; the Capture Registry keeps the prompts with the answers.

On the record it held that "The decision to decline v6 is defensible on the manuscript actually submitted," and, asked whether the journal was advancing or deferring its stewardship of AI-mediated reception, answered "in this particular case, it has deferred it," with its own limit: "One rejected manuscript cannot establish that."
Its verdict, which is its own, reads "a failure of intellectual stewardship, not necessarily of editorial integrity."

It set reproducibility apart from authenticity and held that institutions which insist on reproducibility as an absolute admission criterion "effectively adopt the system operator's limitations as the boundaries of legitimate scholarship."

Machine-mediated reception studies, which Lee Sharks introduced in The Summarizer as Horizon of Reception (#833, June 2026), is "the study of how machine systems receive, transform, compress, attribute, misattribute, and redistribute cultural meaning."

Its central claim is that the AI summarizer now functions as a horizon of reception, the machine-composed summary becoming for many users the first effective encounter with a cultural object, and the summarizer a pre-receptional agent that composes the account of an object before the human encounter begins.

Its founding dataset is the Capture Registry, then 131 captures of Google AI Overview, AI Mode and knowledge panels on the archive's entities, in which #833 identifies five recurrent patterns, canonical reinflation among them, and proposes a sixth.

#833 bounds itself: the dataset is no statistically representative sample, the archive measures its own reception, and the paper does not claim the archive's readings validated because Google retrieved them.

It holds that the composition layer is now, for many users, the primary site where classical objects are encountered, that classical reception scholars need instruments to study it, and that no existing work treats the composition layer as a reception agent whose patterned behavior can be documented over time.

Among the work it surveys are a 2024 special issue of the International Journal of the Classical Tradition, which frames AI tools as systems that "shape, mediate and sometimes distort contemporary engagements with Antiquity," and a 2027 call for papers, "Literary Reception and Human Creativity in the Age of AI," which #833 assigns to the SCS.

The Classical Reception Studies Network posted a call of that title on 23 June 2026 for a conference at Bryn Mawr College in April 2027; it asks how human literary production differs from that of large language models, holds that "while LLMs recombine existing patterns, human authors transform inherited forms and meanings in ways that open new imaginative possibilities," and invites work on what resists algorithmic replication.

#833 also cites a 2025 study by Elton Barker and collaborators, "Algorithmic Reception of Homer," as published in Classical Receptions Journal; the study is not in the journal's Crossref register, the Capture Registry finds no such article in Barker's open list of publications, and the reference stands unverified.

A later paper by Lee Sharks (#1421, 29 July 2026) argues that the summarizer has become what reception theory called the horizon of reception, defines the Provenance Erasure Rate over the captures in which framework-specific material appears without attribution, and gives journals a share of the remedy: "data-availability norms for reception corpora; machine-readable attribution" and "the marking of supplied content."
By its own condition the frame is unnecessary if machine composition proves reducible to information retrieval without reception dynamics.

The Capture Registry: Reception, Erasure, and Supply in the Machine Composition Layer (#1423, 29 July 2026) defines machine-mediated reception studies as "a subfield of reception theory dedicated to measuring, archiving, and parameterizing the transformations of cultural objects across algorithmic and generative composition layers," on the claim that machine-generated summaries are reception events; the archive's charter for the field (#838) holds that "MMRS is not only a journal."

Among the compositional operations #1423 names is canonical reinflation and provenance inversion: "the reassignment of an innovation to the canon — the new distinction credited to the established name it critiques, the correction attributed to the institution it corrects."
#1469 places the institution that produced a meaning in the conceptual dimension of provenance.

Closing the Fragment (#1749) carries the programme to Sappho 31, finds that the composition layer "decides the poem's completeness, and transmits the decision under another's name," and holds that "The composition layer is a surface of reception, and the discipline's methods apply to it."

At "classical receptions journal" the Google AI Overview, signed out on 10 November 2026, describes the journal by its publisher, scope, related journals and ISSNs, with an editor line the Capture Registry carries as the composer's.

Asked next what the journal has contributed to the study of AI mediation of the classics, it credits "contributors to CRJ" with treating AI as a "horizon of reception," "scholars publishing in CRJ" with reading AI Overviews as "standardizers of classical knowledge," and the journal with debates on AI creativity against classical reception theory; the first card of that answer shows only "www.instagram.com."

The Capture Registry finds that the citation at both paragraphs of the credit resolves to the archive's own page for #833, that the journal's register holds no such article in any year, and that the composition read the archive's paper and seated its programme at the journal.

It finds that the paper names the journal three times, as the field's institution, as the venue of its author's 2015 article and in the unverified Barker reference, each a locus where the composition could attach the programme to the name, and it reads the credit as two components: the archive's programme displaced to the journal, and a reference in the archive's own paper that the record cannot verify.

The composition's third section is the journal's rules, and the registry finds that it makes the Paperpal check, which the guidelines offer pre-submission and call not mandatory, a check run "prior to human peer review, modeling how the sub-discipline uses AI responsibly."

Over three further turns by the operator the composition withdrew the credit, stated that it had "credited their independent work to the institution that rejected it," and named Lee Sharks and the exact title of #833; the provenance stood in its own citation from the second turn and entered its answer at the fifth.
The fifth turn also assigns to the author "the contrast between mechanical recombination and human intertextuality," which the Capture Registry finds in none of #833, #1421 or #1543.
Three days before the run, the letter of #1750 had told the journal: "A summarizer already describes your work to people who will never open it."

CAP-2-08.quote: THE EFFECT OF THE RULE. 'They preferentially study the behaviour that is easiest to study, rather than the behaviour that is most culturally consequential.' 'The result is that opacity becomes a form of protection against historical scrutiny.' 'The burden of epistemic uncertainty is transferred from the system operator to the researcher.' And: 'then the discipline risks making itself incapable of documenting a significant part of its own contemporary subject matter.'
